questions.question: In vanilla gradient descent, what does the learning rate control?

options.text: The number of training epochs
The step size taken in the direction of the negative gradient
The number of parameters in the model
The batch size used during training

questions.explanation: The learning rate α scales the gradient to determine how far each parameter update moves in the negative gradient direction.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) over full-batch gradient descent?

options.text: SGD always converges to a lower loss
SGD updates parameters more frequently and scales to large datasets
SGD does not require a learning rate
SGD computes the exact true gradient

questions.explanation: SGD uses a single sample (or mini-batch) per update, enabling faster updates and tractable training on large datasets, at the cost of gradient noise.

questions.question: Which NumPy operation computes the element-wise product of two arrays of identical shape?

options.text: np.dot(a, b)
a @ b
a * b
np.matmul(a, b)

questions.explanation: The * operator performs element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication in NumPy, whereas np.dot and @ perform matrix multiplication.

questions.question: What is the purpose of tf.GradientTape?

options.text: To record operations for automatic differentiation
To save model weights to disk
To accelerate training on GPU only
To visualize training metrics

questions.explanation: tf.GradientTape records forward operations so gradients can be computed via reverse-mode autodiff when tape.gradient() is called.

questions.question: Which factor is generally NOT considered a primary driver of the deep learning revolution of the 2010s?

options.text: Availability of large labeled datasets (e.g. ImageNet)
GPU-accelerated parallel computation
Quantum computing hardware
Algorithmic advances (ReLU, dropout, batch norm)

questions.explanation: The deep learning revolution was driven by data, compute (GPUs), and algorithmic advances. Quantum computing was not a contributor.

questions.question: Given `a` with shape (3, 1) and `b` with shape (1, 4), what is the shape of `a + b` after NumPy broadcasting?

options.text: Error — shapes are incompatible

questions.explanation: Broadcasting stretches each dimension of size 1 to match the other operand, so (3,1) and (1,4) both become (3,4). A common student mistake is to assume the arrays must have identical shapes before addition.

questions.question: You set a very large learning rate and the loss starts oscillating and then diverges to NaN. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The step size is too large, causing updates to overshoot the minimum and amplify each iteration
The model has too few parameters to fit the data
The batch size is too small to estimate the gradient
The dataset is not shuffled between epochs

questions.explanation: With a learning rate above the stability threshold (roughly 2/L for an L-smooth loss), each step overshoots the minimum by more than it corrects, producing growing oscillations that eventually overflow to NaN. Shrinking the learning rate or using a schedule typically fixes it.

questions.question: Inside a `tf.GradientTape()` block, you compute `y = x * x` where `x` is a `tf.constant`. Calling `tape.gradient(y, x)` returns `None`. Why?

options.text: Gradients with respect to non-trainable tensors are not tracked by default; `x` must be a `tf.Variable` or watched explicitly via `tape.watch(x)`
`tf.GradientTape` only records operations on GPU tensors
`y = x * x` has a zero gradient at the origin, so TensorFlow returns `None` as an optimization
The tape was not placed inside a `@tf.function`

questions.explanation: By default, `tf.GradientTape` only records operations on trainable `tf.Variable`s. Constants are ignored unless you call `tape.watch(x)` to add them explicitly — a common gotcha when first learning autodiff in TF 2.x.

questions.question: Why is initializing all weights to zero a bad idea for a multi-layer neural network?

options.text: Zero weights cause division-by-zero errors during training
All neurons in a layer compute the same function and receive identical gradient updates, so the network never learns diverse features
TensorFlow raises an error if weights are initialized to zero
Zero initialization causes exploding gradients in the first backward pass

questions.explanation: With all-zero weights, every neuron in a layer produces the same output and receives the same gradient — this is called the 'symmetry problem'. The network effectively behaves as if it has one neuron per layer no matter how wide it is. Random initialization (e.g., He or Xavier) breaks this symmetry.

questions.question: A NumPy array `a` is created with `np.zeros((1000, 1000), order='C')`. Which access pattern will be faster and why?

options.text: Iterating over rows (a[i, :]) is faster because C-order stores rows contiguously in memory, enabling CPU cache line prefetching
Iterating over columns (a[:, j]) is faster because C-order prioritizes column access
Both patterns are equally fast because NumPy always optimizes memory access
Neither is fast — NumPy arrays of this size always use disk-backed storage

questions.explanation: C-order (row-major) arrays store elements row by row in contiguous memory. Accessing a[i, :] reads consecutive memory addresses, which the CPU cache prefetcher handles efficiently. Column access (a[:, j]) jumps 1000 elements between reads, causing frequent cache misses. For column-major access patterns, use order='F' (Fortran order). This is covered in Chapter 3 on NumPy internals.

questions.question: Adam combines ideas from two earlier optimizers. Which two techniques does Adam unify?

options.text: Momentum (first moment of the gradient) and RMSprop-style adaptive learning rates (second moment of the gradient)
AdaGrad's accumulated gradient and Nesterov's look-ahead correction
Learning rate warmup and cosine annealing
Weight decay and gradient clipping

questions.explanation: Adam maintains two exponential moving averages: m_t (first moment, like momentum) and v_t (second moment, like RMSprop). It then applies bias correction to both before computing the update. This is why Adam often works well out-of-the-box — it adapts per-parameter learning rates while also smoothing gradient noise via momentum.

questions.question: You decorate a function with `@tf.function` and call it first with a tensor of shape (32, 10) and then with shape (64, 10). What happens on the second call?

options.text: TensorFlow retraces the function because the input signature changed, creating a second cached graph
TensorFlow reuses the first graph since both inputs are 2-D tensors
TensorFlow raises a ValueError because the shape doesn't match the first trace
The function runs in eager mode since @tf.function only traces once

questions.explanation: tf.function traces a new concrete function for each unique input signature (shape + dtype). The second call has a different first dimension (64 vs 32), so TF retraces and caches a second graph. This is why you may see 'retracing' warnings if you call a tf.function with many different shapes — use input_signature to constrain it. Covered in Section 4.4.3.

questions.question: You are building a deep network where all hidden layers use ReLU activation. Which weight initialization scheme should you use and why?

options.text: Xavier/Glorot initialization (std = sqrt(2 / (fan_in + fan_out))), because it balances variance across layers for symmetric activations
He/Kaiming initialization (std = sqrt(2 / fan_in)), because ReLU zeros out half its inputs and He accounts for this by doubling the variance
All-zeros initialization, because ReLU outputs are always non-negative and symmetry is not required
Uniform random initialization in [-1, 1], because larger initial values help ReLU escape the dead-neuron region

questions.explanation: Xavier initialization was derived assuming symmetric activations (tanh, sigmoid) where the effective fan is the average of fan_in and fan_out. ReLU kills roughly half its inputs, effectively halving the variance. He initialization corrects for this by using only fan_in (the incoming connections), setting std = sqrt(2/fan_in). Using Xavier with ReLU results in variance shrinking layer by layer, making very deep networks hard to train. In Keras, this is `kernel_initializer='he_normal'`.

questions.question: What is the key computational difference between standard Momentum and Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG)?

options.text: NAG uses a larger momentum coefficient (γ > 1) to accelerate convergence, whereas standard Momentum clips γ to [0, 1]
NAG computes the gradient at the look-ahead position (θ − γv) before updating, whereas standard Momentum computes the gradient at the current position θ
NAG normalizes the gradient by its running variance, whereas standard Momentum only accumulates the first moment
NAG applies momentum only on the bias terms, whereas standard Momentum applies it uniformly to all parameters

questions.explanation: Standard Momentum first computes the gradient at the current position θ_t, then moves in the direction of the accumulated velocity v. NAG reverses this order: it first takes the momentum step to the 'look-ahead' position θ_t − γv_t, then evaluates the gradient there. This allows the gradient to 'correct' an overly large momentum step before it is taken, giving NAG better convergence properties on convex problems and making it the preferred variant in practice (e.g., the `nesterov=True` flag in `tf.keras.optimizers.SGD`). Covered in Section 2.5.2.
